newsitem.title: UK: Northern Irish New Year brings IRA bomb alert.
newsitem.headline: Northern Irish New Year brings IRA bomb alert.

text.p: The IRA launched the New Year with a bomb alert at a hotel packed with revellers.

As bomb disposal experts tackled a suspected landmine left in a van, the province's leading Protestant politician warned that the Irish Republican Army had no intention of calling off its guerrilla war against Britain.

"There have been several attempts at major terrorist attacks in Northern Ireland (in recent months). It underlines the complete fatuity of the suggestions that there was about to be a ceasefire," Ulster Unionist Party chief David Trimble said.
"There's no indication whatsoever that the IRA are contemplating politics, every indication that they are trying to step up their activity," he told BBC Radio.

Police said a man using an IRA identity codeword had telephoned the media late on Tuesday saying that guerrillas had abandoned" the device in the grounds of Belfast Castle, a 19th century former private mansion.
Police officers on high alert during renewed guerrilla tension had already become suspicious of a van parked in the hotel grounds and called in the bomb squad.
A bride and groom, their guests and others attending New Year's Eve receptions were among those led out of the building.
Security has been stepped up across Northern Ireland and in mainland Britain since the IRA abandoned a ceasefire last February in a 27-year campaign to end British rule.
The IRA set off a wave of bombs in British cities and killed a soldier at British army headquarters south of Belfast last October, dashing hopes of an early end to violence.
Tension increased recently with signs that pro-British Loyalist guerrillas might end a two-year truce. Booby trap bombs were placed under cars belonging to senior republicans, injuring one of them.

Loyalist extremist commanders have refused to state whether their ceasefire is over but the attacks have triggered fears that deadlocked political efforts for peace might be further clouded by a new cycle of tit-for-tat violence.
